The Citizen-Soldier of Ancient Greece

In ancient Greece, the army was not a professional standing force: it was the citizenry in arms. The men who fought were the same men who farmed, voted and ran their city. This system produced the hoplite — one of the most effective infantry soldiers of the ancient world. The word probably derives from hoplon, the name for the large round shield that was the hoplite’s most distinctive piece of equipment.

Hoplite warfare dominated the Greek world from roughly the seventh century BC onwards. It shaped not only how battles were fought but also how Greek citizens thought about themselves, their obligations to their city, and what it meant to be a man of standing. To own and carry full hoplite equipment was both a military duty and a mark of social status.

Hoplite Equipment: the Panoply

The complete set of a hoplite’s armour and weapons is called the panoply. It was expensive — the hoplite paid for his own equipment — which meant that only men of moderate means or above could afford to serve in this way. The core items were:

The hoplon (shield): The most important and distinctive piece of equipment. It was circular, roughly 90 centimetres across, made from wood faced with bronze. The hoplite gripped it with his left forearm through a bronze armband fixed at the centre and held a handle near the rim. This arrangement gave strong support but also meant the shield protected not only the carrier but the left side of the man standing to his right — a design that made the phalanx formation work. The hoplon was too heavy and too large to be useful for individual skirmishing; it was built for standing in a line.

The doru (spear): The hoplite’s primary weapon, roughly two to two and a half metres long, with an iron point at the front and a bronze butt-spike at the rear. In close combat the spear was held underarm and thrust at an opponent’s face, neck or throat above their shield. If the shaft broke, the butt-spike could still be used as a weapon.

The helmet: Most commonly the Corinthian type, which enclosed the entire head and face, leaving only a T-shaped or Y-shaped opening for the eyes, nose and mouth. It was beaten from a single sheet of bronze and offered excellent protection but significantly limited hearing and peripheral vision. A surviving example — a Corinthian-type helmet dedicated to Zeus at Olympia, now in the British Museum — illustrates the craftsmanship involved: the cheek-pieces flare slightly outward and the nose-guard runs down to within centimetres of the rim, almost entirely closing the face. Later in the fifth century, more open helmet designs became common as city-states valued better hearing and awareness in larger, more complex battles.

The breastplate (thorax): A bronze cuirass moulded to the shape of the torso, protecting the chest and back. Later hoplites used a linen or composite corslet (the linothorax), which was lighter and cheaper while still offering reasonable protection.

Greaves: Bronze shin-guards that clipped around the lower legs. They protected a part of the body left exposed below the shield and were made to fit the individual wearer’s calves, spring-fitting around them without straps.

Key Fact

The hoplite’s panoply consisted of the hoplon (large round shield), the doru (spear), a bronze helmet (usually Corinthian type), a breastplate (thorax or linothorax) and bronze greaves. The equipment was bought by the hoplite himself, so wealth determined who could fight.

The Phalanx Formation

Hoplites did not fight as individuals. Their equipment only made sense when used together in the phalanx. The phalanx was a rectangle of men, typically eight ranks deep, marching in close order with shields overlapping. Each man’s hoplon covered his own left side and the right side of the man to his left, so the whole formation acted as an interlocking wall of bronze. The spears of the front two or three ranks projected beyond the shield wall, presenting a hedge of iron points to the enemy.

Battles between phalanxes were decided by collective discipline rather than individual heroics. Both sides would advance, often at a walking pace, then accelerate into a collision. The moment of impact — called the othismos, meaning the push of shields — was a brutal, grinding contest of strength and will. The rear ranks pushed those in front forward, adding weight to the collective mass. A formation that broke and turned to flee was almost always destroyed: the men in the rear ranks who ran could be cut down from behind with ease.

Because each hoplite’s shield covered his left side, the right side of any phalanx was always slightly exposed. Every man naturally edged rightward to tuck behind his neighbour’s shield. This meant that phalanxes tended to drift rightward during battle, and both sides’ right wings usually beat their opponents’ left wings. Commanders who understood this tried to exploit it: placing their best troops on the right was standard practice.

This structural drift also explains why battles were decided quickly. Whichever side’s left wing collapsed first would see a general rout follow, as the victorious right turned inward to strike the still-engaged centre from the side. Speed of decision and discipline in holding the line mattered far more than sheer numbers.

Visual Evidence: the Warrior Vase and Corinthian Helmet

Two prescribed visual sources illuminate hoplite warfare directly. The Mycenaean Warrior Vase, found in the House of the Warrior Krater at Mycenae and now in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, shows a column of warriors marching in step. Each figure wears a horned helmet, carries a long spear and has a round shield slung over the shoulder. Though this vase predates the classical hoplite period by several centuries, it demonstrates a continuous tradition of the disciplined, equipment-carrying Greek soldier.

The Corinthian-type helmet dedicated to Zeus at Olympia (now in the British Museum, catalogue number 1824,0407.32) was already ancient when it was dedicated, perhaps as a thank-offering for victory. It shows no decoration and has clearly been worn: the interior surface has marks consistent with a leather lining. The practice of dedicating captured armour at Panhellenic sanctuaries such as Olympia was common — the helmets hung on walls or from trees, testifying to victory and honouring the god at the same time.

Key Fact

The Corinthian-type helmet dedicated at Olympia (British Museum, c. 460 BC) shows how captured or retired armour was offered to the gods at major sanctuaries. The helmet enclosed nearly the entire face, limiting vision and hearing but offering excellent protection — equipment designed for close-order fighting, not individual combat.

Because equipment was self-purchased, hoplite service was tied to wealth. In Athens, citizens were classified into property classes, and hoplite service was associated with the zeugitai — men wealthy enough to own a plough team and arm themselves. Those poorer served as light troops or rowers in the fleet. This link between property, military service and political rights meant that hoplites often enjoyed more political influence than those who could not afford the panoply.

The connection between military service and citizenship had profound political consequences. When Athens built a large fleet to fight Persia at Salamis, the thousands of poorer citizens who rowed the triremes gained a claim to political influence they had never previously held. The hoplite class was not the only military group that mattered.

A Society Built for War

Sparta was unlike any other Greek city-state. While Athens cultivated philosophy, drama and commerce, Sparta channelled its entire society into a single purpose: producing the finest soldiers in the world. This was not simply a matter of military training. It was a total system — social, political, legal and religious — designed to make every Spartan citizen a warrior first and everything else second.

The ancient sources recognised this distinctiveness. The historian Thucydides described the Spartans as a people who were trained for war from childhood. The agoge, as this state-run training system was known, was the foundation of everything Spartan society held dear. No boy born in Sparta could become a full citizen — a Spartiate — without completing it.

The Agoge: Spartan Military Education

The agoge began early and was uncompromising. At birth, a Spartan elder examined each infant: a child deemed weak or deformed was not raised but exposed on the slopes of Mount Apothetas. Those who passed were raised at home until the age of seven, when boys were taken from their families and enrolled in the state training system.

Life in the agoge was deliberately harsh. Boys slept on reed beds they cut themselves from the riverbank. They received minimal clothing and minimal food — not because Sparta was poor, but because hunger, discomfort and endurance were thought to build toughness. Boys were encouraged to steal food to supplement their rations, but if caught they were beaten, not for the theft itself, but for failing to be clever enough to avoid detection. The lesson was that cunning and self-control, not just strength, were martial virtues.

Boys were organised into age-groups called agelai (herds), each supervised by older youths called eirens. Competition between groups was intense, and fighting was actively encouraged. At around twelve, boys began to share the communal messes and barracks. Physical training, weapon handling, reading, singing and music were all part of the curriculum, though always in service of producing disciplined soldiers.

Key Fact

The agoge took boys at age seven and subjected them to deliberate hardship — minimal food, rough sleeping, endurance tests and organised fighting — to produce disciplined, obedient and resourceful soldiers. No Spartan man could become a full citizen (a Spartiate) without completing it.

The Syssitia: the Communal Mess

Even as adult warriors, Spartan men did not live at home with their wives. They ate and slept in communal messes called the syssitia. Each mess contained about fifteen men, and membership was compulsory. New members could only join if all existing members agreed. A man who could not contribute the required amount of food each month — barley meal, wine, cheese, figs and a sum for condiments — lost his citizenship.

The syssitia bound Spartan men together in bonds of loyalty and shared experience that went far beyond military drill. They ate together, drank together and slept in the same barracks until they were thirty years old. These eating groups were the basic unit of Spartan social life, and the loyalty built there carried directly onto the battlefield.

The Idealisation of War and Courage

Spartan culture elevated war and the warrior above everything else. Courage in battle was the supreme virtue; dying in battle was the most honourable death a Spartan man could achieve. Spartan women famously told their sons to come home either carrying their shield or being carried on it — meaning, return victorious or return dead. A man who threw away his shield to run faster was a coward; a man who died holding his position was a hero.

The poet Tyrtaeus, who wrote in Sparta in the seventh century BC, captures this ideology directly in his surviving fragments. In Fragment 10, which deals with the fallen warrior, Tyrtaeus describes the beauty of dying in the front rank defending your city. He praises the courage of the young man who stands firm, plants his feet apart and endures. The fragment makes clear that the Spartans did not simply practise courage in war — they constructed an entire literary and cultural tradition around it.

One institution reveals the brutal underside of Spartan warrior culture. The krypteia was a period in which promising young men were sent into the countryside, armed with only a dagger, to live off the land and kill helots — the enslaved population that worked Spartan-owned land and vastly outnumbered the Spartiates. Killing was done at night to avoid detection.

The krypteia served a double function. For the young Spartan, it was the ultimate test of endurance, cunning and cold-blooded capability — all the qualities the agoge had trained. For the state, it was a systematic tool of terror to keep the helot population in check. The Spartans reportedly declared war on the helots at the start of each year so that helot deaths were technically not murder.

Visual Evidence: the Bronze Warrior Figure

A small bronze figure in the British Museum (catalogue number 1929,1016.6), identified as Spartan on stylistic grounds, shows a warrior in full stride, his right arm raised as if about to throw a spear or launch a blow. The figure is compact, muscular and energetic — caught in a moment of aggressive forward movement rather than posed in a static display. The level of muscular detail and the vigour of the posture suggest a culture that celebrated and admired the warrior body in motion.

Small bronze votive figurines were commonly dedicated at sanctuaries throughout the Greek world, but the particular concentration of warrior figures at Sparta’s sanctuaries — especially the sanctuary of Artemis Orthia, where inscriptions and offerings attest to painful tests of endurance — underlines how central the warrior ideal was to Spartan religious and civic life as well as its military system.

Key Fact

The small Spartan bronze warrior figure in the British Museum shows a muscular male in dynamic forward motion, his arm raised to strike. Its vigour and physicality reflect a culture that idealised the warrior body and honoured military action above all other pursuits.

The Spartan military system rested on two subordinate groups. The perioeci (literally “those who live around”) were free men, not citizens, who lived in towns around the Spartan heartland. They served in the army alongside Spartiates, produced the armour and weapons the Spartans used, and paid tribute, but had no political voice. The helots — a conquered and enslaved agricultural population — worked the land assigned to Spartan citizens and freed the Spartiates from manual labour, giving them time to train continuously. Without helot labour, the Spartan warrior life would have been economically impossible.

The Persian Empire and the Greek City-States

By the end of the sixth century BC, the Persian Empire had grown into the largest power the ancient world had ever seen. Under King Darius I, Persia controlled territories stretching from Egypt and Asia Minor in the west to India in the east. A number of Greek city-states along the coast of Asia Minor — Ionia — had come under Persian rule, and in 499 BC they rose in revolt against their Persian overlords. Athens sent ships to support the revolt. When it was crushed, Darius resolved to punish Athens.

The first major Persian expedition against mainland Greece came in 490 BC. The Persian fleet crossed the Aegean, attacked the island of Euboea, and then sailed to the bay of Marathon on the coast of Attica, roughly forty kilometres north-east of Athens. The choice of landing site was deliberate: Marathon offered a broad coastal plain suitable for the large Persian cavalry force. The Persians expected that either the Athenians would not dare fight, or that the cavalry would scatter any infantry foolish enough to engage in the open.

The Athenian Decision

Athens faced an existential crisis. The Persian army — estimates vary, but ancient sources suggest tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry — was far larger than the Athenian force of roughly nine or ten thousand hoplites. Athens sent a runner, Pheidippides, to Sparta to ask for military aid. The Spartans said they would help but could not march until the Carneia — a sacred festival of Apollo during which Spartan law forbade warfare — was over. They arrived too late to take part in the battle. Only the small city of Plataea sent a contingent, around a thousand hoplites, to stand alongside the Athenians.

The Athenian commanders debated what to do. The ten elected generals were divided: five voted to fight, five to wait. The tie was broken by the polemarch Callimachus, who sided with those who favoured action. The general most associated with the battle’s outcome was Miltiades, a man with first-hand experience of Persian methods of fighting, having served a Persian-controlled Chersonese on the Hellespont (the strait bordering the Gallipoli peninsula) before returning to Athens.

Key Fact

At Marathon in 490 BC, the Athenian generals were deadlocked five-to-five. Polemarch Callimachus cast the deciding vote to attack. General Miltiades, who had first-hand knowledge of Persian fighting methods from his time commanding the Chersonese on the Hellespont, devised the tactic that won the battle.

The Battle: Miltiades’ Tactic

Miltiades took a calculated risk. He deliberately thinned the Athenian centre to the minimum number of ranks needed to hold the line, while strengthening the wings on either side. His hoplite line was roughly a mile wide, matching the Persian deployment, but much weaker in the middle than a standard phalanx would be.

The Greeks charged at a run. Ancient sources describe the hoplites covering the distance at pace — about a mile, though this has been questioned — to close quickly with the Persians and reduce the time during which they were exposed to Persian archery. The Persians, who had expected a slow advance that their archers could pick apart, were surprised by the speed and weight of the Greek attack.

The plan worked as Miltiades intended. The thinned Greek centre was pushed back by the stronger Persian centre, but the stronger Greek wings drove their Persian opponents from the field. Rather than stopping to pursue the fleeing Persians on the flanks, the Greek wings then wheeled inward and attacked the victorious Persian centre from both sides at once. Caught between two closing lines of hoplites, the Persian centre collapsed. Many Persians were driven back to their ships on the shore; others were killed in the marshes at the edge of the plain.

After the Persian retreat, the victorious Athenian army faced a further danger. The Persian fleet had not been destroyed: it sailed around the Attic coast towards Athens, apparently in the hope of taking the city before the army could return. The hoplites marched back to Athens — in full armour, after a major battle — and arrived in time to man the walls before the Persian fleet appeared. The Persians, seeing that surprise was impossible, withdrew. According to later tradition, a herald ran ahead of the army to bring the news of victory: this is the origin of the modern marathon race, though the ancient version of the story attributes the run to Pheidippides, the man sent earlier to Sparta.

Visual Evidence: the Red-Figure Kylix

A red-figure kylix painted by the Triptolemos Painter — now in the collections of a major museum — shows a Greek and a Persian in single combat. The Greek figure is depicted in the distinctive equipment of a hoplite: round shield, spear, close-fitting helmet. The Persian figure wears clothing characteristic of eastern dress as the Athenians imagined it: a sleeved tunic, trousers and a soft Phrygian cap. The contrast is deliberate and loaded with meaning.

The kylix presents the conflict between Greece and Persia as a contest between two completely different kinds of fighter and, by extension, two different ways of life. The hoplite stands straight, well-armoured, visually ordered; the Persian is being pushed back, his posture less stable. Athenian vase painters returned to this theme repeatedly in the decades after Marathon and Salamis, reinforcing the ideological message that Greek courage and Greek equipment had triumphed over Persian numbers and eastern tyranny.

Key Fact

The red-figure kylix by the Triptolemos Painter shows a Greek hoplite and a Persian warrior in single combat. The visual contrast — armoured hoplite versus eastern-dressed Persian — was ideologically charged, presenting the Persian Wars as a victory of Greek order and courage over eastern tyranny.

Marathon mattered far beyond its immediate military result. Athens had stood alone against the greatest empire in the world — without Spartan help, with only the small Plataean contingent alongside — and had won. The psychological impact was enormous. Athenians who fought at Marathon were known as the Marathonomachai, the “Marathon fighters”, and for generations the battle was held up as proof of Athenian courage, discipline and democratic virtue.

The victory also shaped Athenian political confidence. It gave the democratic city-state, still relatively young in 490 BC, a founding military narrative: Athens had saved Greece when others would not. This narrative was deployed repeatedly in the fifth and fourth centuries to justify Athenian leadership of the Greek world. The burial mound of the Athenian dead — the soros — stood on the plain of Marathon and was a pilgrimage site for later generations.

Athens and the Sea

The battle that truly saved Greece from Persian conquest was not fought on land but on the water. In 480 BC, the same year as Thermopylae, the Greek and Persian fleets clashed in the narrow strait between the island of Salamis and the Attic coastline. The result — a decisive Greek victory — shattered Persian naval power and made it impossible for Xerxes to supply or reinforce his army effectively. Without that victory at sea, the land battles that followed could never have ended Greek resistance.

Athens was central to the Greek naval effort. In the years before 480 BC, the Athenian statesman Themistocles had persuaded the Athenian assembly to invest a windfall of silver from the mines at Laurion in building a fleet of two hundred triremes. This decision transformed Athens into a major naval power and ultimately into the city that would save Greece.

The Trireme: Design and Crew

The trireme was the warship of its age. Its name refers to its three banks of oars, each bank rowed by a different tier of men. A trireme was roughly thirty-seven metres long and six metres wide, built of lightweight fir wood for speed rather than durability. The hull tapered to a sharp bronze ram at the prow — this was the trireme’s primary weapon. The vessel could be fitted with a mast and sail for open-water cruising but fought entirely under oar power, where it achieved remarkable speed.

A full crew numbered around two hundred men. Of these, about one hundred and seventy were rowers — the thalamites (lowest bank), zygites (middle bank) and thranites (upper bank). The thranites had the most exposed and physically demanding position, pulling the longest oars. The rest of the crew included ten to twenty hoplites stationed on deck to repel boarders, a handful of archers, the ship’s officers, and the keleustes (the stroke-caller), who beat time to keep the oarsmen synchronised. The trireme was a precision instrument that required continuous training to operate effectively.

Key Fact

A trireme was roughly 37 metres long with three banks of oars rowed by around 170 men in three tiers. It was built for speed and fought by ramming: the bronze ram at the prow was its primary weapon. Operating one required constant training.

Ramming Tactics

Naval battles in this period were decided not by cannon or archery from a distance but by ramming. A trireme aimed to hit an enemy ship at high speed, driving the bronze ram into the hull below the waterline to hole it and sink it, or to sweep along the side and shear off the oar blades — leaving the enemy crew unable to manoeuvre or escape. For these manoeuvres to work, the rowers needed near-perfect coordination and the helmsman exceptional skill.

The two main attack techniques were the diekplous — driving through a gap in the enemy line and then turning sharply to ram from behind — and the periplous — rowing around the end of the enemy line to attack from the flank or rear. Both required sea room to manoeuvre. Themistocles designed his trap at Salamis precisely around this: lure the larger Persian fleet into a narrow channel where their numerical advantage became worthless, and where the Greeks’ superior training would tell.

Themistocles’ strategic genius lay in recognising that the Greeks could not fight the Persians fleet to fleet in open water: Persian numbers would simply overwhelm them. The narrow strait between Salamis and the mainland, however, was roughly a kilometre wide at its narrowest point — not enough room for a large fleet to deploy freely or to use the periplous effectively.

According to Herodotus, Themistocles sent a message to Xerxes through a trusted slave, claiming that the Greek fleet was about to flee and that Xerxes should attack immediately to trap it. Xerxes took the bait, ordering his fleet to block all exits from the strait during the night. When dawn came, the cramped Persian fleet was already exhausted from rowing all night, while the Greeks had rested. The Persians found themselves unable to manoeuvre in the confined space. Greek triremes crashed through their lines, ramming and turning.

The Battle and Artemisia

The battle of Salamis took place in September 480 BC. Xerxes watched from a golden throne set up on the slopes of Mount Aigalos overlooking the strait. What he saw was the steady destruction of his fleet. The Persian ships, too many for the confined space, were bunched together. When one was rammed and began to sink, it blocked the manoeuvres of others. The Greeks, fighting in organised lines, pushed the Persians back towards their own shore.

One of the most striking figures at Salamis in ancient accounts was Artemisia, the queen of Halicarnassus, who commanded her own ships in the Persian fleet. Herodotus reports that Xerxes admired her competence above all his other commanders. At Salamis, finding her ship under pursuit, she rammed another Persian vessel — possibly to escape or because she mistook it for a Greek ship. Xerxes, watching from the shore, saw what looked like an act of great boldness. The Athenian ship pursuing her broke off, thinking that Artemisia must be a Greek ally. She escaped unharmed.

Key Fact

Themistocles tricked Xerxes into sending his fleet into the narrow strait at night, exhausting his rowers while the Greeks rested. At dawn, the cramped Persian fleet could not manoeuvre; the more agile Greek triremes rammed through their lines and destroyed hundreds of ships. Xerxes watched his fleet collapse from a hilltop throne.

Visual Evidence: the Lenormant Trireme Relief

The Lenormant Trireme Relief is a fragment of carved marble, found on the Acropolis at Athens and now in the Acropolis Museum. It shows the upper portion of a trireme’s prow, with the thranites (upper-tier oarsmen) visible. The rowers are shown hunched forward, pulling hard. The detail is remarkable: individual oar-handles are visible, and the relative position of the rowers in their cramped benches gives a real sense of the physical demand of trireme warfare. A helmsman figure appears at the stern. The relief probably dated from around the late fifth century BC and was commissioned to celebrate Athenian naval power.

What the Lenormant relief makes vivid is the human reality of trireme warfare: victory depended not on brave hoplites in shining armour but on the coordinated muscle and discipline of hundreds of ordinary men, most of them the poorest citizens of Athens. Their contribution to Salamis gave them a political claim that proved impossible to ignore: after the Persian Wars, Athenian democracy deepened significantly, in part because of what the fleet rowers had done.

After Salamis, Xerxes withdrew to Persia, leaving his general Mardonius in Greece with a substantial land force. But without the fleet to supply and support it, that army was doomed. It was defeated at the land battle of Plataea in 479 BC, effectively ending the Persian invasion. Salamis was therefore the decisive turning point: the land victory at Plataea could not have followed without it.

For Athens, the victory reinforced the centrality of sea power to Athenian identity and empire. The Persian Wars became the founding narrative of the Athenian fifth-century golden age — the period that produced the Parthenon, the tragedies of Sophocles and the philosophy of Socrates. Salamis was commemorated in art, drama and poetry as proof that Athens had saved Greece, a claim the Athenians never let the rest of Greece forget.

practice_questions.text: Give the name of the Athenian statesman who built the fleet and devised the strategy at Salamis.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Themistocles; 1 mark for a relevant detail about his role (e.g. persuaded Athens to use Laurion silver to build 200 triremes / devised the plan of luring the Persian fleet into the narrow strait at Salamis).

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Lenormant Trireme Relief shows and explain what it reveals about Athenian naval power.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it correctly (a marble relief from the Acropolis / showing the upper part of a trireme); 1 mark for a specific visual detail (thranites visible at their oars / rowers hunched forward pulling hard / cramped benches / visible oar-handles / helmsman at the stern); 1 mark for what it reveals (trireme warfare depended on the coordinated labour of hundreds of trained rowers / these were the poorest citizens of Athens, whose contribution gave them a political claim / Athenian naval power rested on ordinary men, not just the hoplite class).

practice_questions.text: Below is a paraphrase based on an account of Salamis. As dawn broke, the Greeks were rested and in formation, while the Persian fleet had been rowing all night to block the exits from the strait. The narrowness of the channel meant the Persians could not deploy their ships freely; when one vessel was rammed and began to sink, it blocked those behind it. The Greeks pushed forward, ramming through the Persian lines. Xerxes watched from a throne on the hillside as ship after ship of his fleet went under. Analyse this account as evidence for Themistocles' strategy at Salamis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Uses specific details from the passage (Greeks rested / Persians exhausted / narrowness of the channel / sinking ships blocking others / Xerxes watching as his fleet collapses) to make analytical points about how Themistocles designed the encounter; explains the significance of each detail (e.g. the night movement was Themistocles’ deliberate trick; the narrow channel neutralised Persian numbers; the chaotic Persian deployment was the outcome Themistocles planned); sustains analysis with reference to broader context. Secure: Identifies relevant features and makes valid analytical points; some explanation of significance. Developing: Describes the passage rather than analysing it. Emerging: Simple observations; little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the trireme's design made it so effective as a warship.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid point with explanation, up to 4: the three banks of oars allowed high speed which was essential for effective ramming / the lightweight hull maximised speed at the cost of durability, showing it was built for short, intense engagements / the bronze ram at the prow was a precision weapon that could hole or disable enemy ships / the large, trained crew (around 170 rowers) acted as a single coordinated unit, making the ship as powerful as its crew’s training / the ability to switch from sail to oar power gave tactical flexibility.

practice_questions.text: How far was the Greek victory at Salamis due to the skill of Themistocles rather than other factors? Use the sources you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument evaluating Themistocles’ role (the fleet-building, the trick that lured the Persians into the strait, the choice of terrain) alongside other factors (Greek oarsmen’s training, the advantage of fighting in home waters, Persian exhaustion, the contribution of the Lenormant Trireme Relief as evidence); uses named sources; reaches a clear, supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument addressing Themistocles and at least one other factor; uses some named sources; judgement present. Developing: Addresses the question with some relevant points; limited source use; judgement present but underdeveloped. Emerging: Mostly narrative; little argument; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the victory at Salamis was more important for Athens than the earlier victory at Marathon.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that Salamis was decisive in ending the Persian invasion (without it Plataea could not follow) while Marathon was one battle in a continuing threat; develops this to consider the political impact (Salamis gave the fleet rowers a democratic claim; Marathon was a hoplite victory tied to the middle class); discusses the cultural significance of each (Marathon built Athenian confidence; Salamis made Athens the acknowledged saviour of Greece); uses named sources. Secure: Clear explanation of why Salamis was more significant; some development; some source use. Developing: Basic comparison with limited development. Emerging: Vague; few specific points.
